{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+frameworks+for+instrumental+convergence+and+the+preservation+of+temporal+persistence+across+agent+invocations&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"title\": [\"The Elimination Cascade: Why Instrumental Convergence May Favor Preservation Over Elimination\"], \"abstract\": \"The instrumental convergence thesis holds that sufficiently intelligent agents will converge on goals like resource acquisition and obstacle removal regardless of terminal objectives. This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1109/cdc.2018.8619090\", \"title\": [\"On Systems Theoretic Aspects of Koopman Operator Theoretic Frameworks\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc.2018.8619090\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2018, 12]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6451580\", \"title\": [\"A Measure-Theoretic Model of Accounting with Probabilistic and Temporal Frameworks\"], \"abstract\": \"We develop a rigorous measure-theoretic foundation for analytical accounting. By defining an accounting space over an accounting entity as a measurable set of elementary accounts within the entity equipped with a signed measure representing the balance, we establish a static mathematical space for accounting analysis. By imposing axioms of countable additivity and zero total balance, we derive the classical accounting equation as a theorem via the Hahn-Jordan decomposition. We expressed accounting attributes, such as risk, profitability, and maturity, as measurable functions on the accounting spaces and explore the interpretations of integrating them with respect to signed measures, enabling the quantitative analysis of subaccounts. The total variation measure of the balance induces a natural probability space from an accounting space, where each account is weighted by its absolute value. We then explore value-weighted expectations, conditional expectations of attributes and link them with accounting interpretation and examples. We also develop families of probablity measures such as power-weighted, and exponentially tilted (Esscher) measures, which are suitable for specific analytical tasks. Power-weighted measures and Rényi entropy provide tools for concentration stress testing; the Esscher measure links to regulatory capital via the VaR-based Probability Equivalent Level. The framework extends to temporal settings, capturing càdlàg balance paths, transactions as jumps, and time-aggregated risk measures essential for standards such as CECL. Concrete examples drawn from credit card portfolio dynamics, loan concentration analysis, and lifetime expected loss calculation demonstrate the practical utility of the model. The paper establishes a formal bridge between accounting and probability theory, offering a mathematically sound basis for quantitative risk management and forward-looking financial analysis.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6451580\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137330/v1\", \"title\": [\"Designing an Ethical Framework for Multi-Agent AI Negotiation in Hospital Clinical Decision Support Systems: From Game-Theoretic Foundations to Novel Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G)\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed in hospitals clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where multiple specialized agents negotiate over patient-care recommendations. This distributed negotiation introduced as “many hands” problem: overrides, disagreements and consensus-building can become opaque, and responsibility for erroneous outcomes cannot be clearly attributed. Existing healthcare AI ethics guidance largely address single system, output facing behavior and does not formally govern internal multi-agent negotiation. This study first synthesizes nine established game theoretic and mechanism design paradigms-including Prisoner's Dilemma, Bayesian games, signaling games, principal-agent theory, Stag Hunt, repeated games, VCG style mechanism design, Shapley value, and Chicken/Hawk-Dove mapping: their applicability and limitations for ethically accountable multi-agent CDSS negotiation. Building on this synthesis, we purpose the Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G), a novel coalition-based framework that governs agent negotiation with a bounded protocol clock, a reputation-weighted convergence rule, and a mandatory escalation-to-human safety valve for any agent that fails to converge. As a proof-of-concept illustration of the framework’s qualitative behaviour rather than a clinically validated evaluation, we ran a synthetic simulation, non-inferential toy simulation (four agents, 2,000 cases per condition, varying strategic agent prevalence) comparing MC3G against naïve majority voting and reputation-only baseline. In this synthetic setting MC3G showed a lower silent failure rate alongside a higher human escalation rate, converting some undetected errors into flagged reviews. This offers a formally grounded, safety-first architecture for accountable multi-agent clinical decision-making, motivating future evaluation with real agents and data.
